## Intent
Hypothesis: making loop1 Halide-expressible enables compiler vectorization of the per-particle math, approaching the streaming ceiling on low-churn workloads while loop2's RNG-order dependency runs as scalar overhead.

## Cache saturation
All measured N (10000–10000000) exceed the L1d spill at N≈963; N=10000 sits below the L2 spill at N≈61680, N≥100000 exceeds it. At every death rate the curve is FLAT across N: at q=0.01 cost holds 8.33–8.96 ns/p with slight overhead amortization from N=10000→100000, then flat through N=10000000. No knee appears at the L2→DRAM transition. Death rate raises the floor without reshaping the curve: the flat level climbs from ~8.3 ns/p (q=0.01) to ~14.2 ns/p (q=0.5), but N-invariance persists at every q.

## Bandwidth
Peak is 8.21 GB/s at N=1000000, q=0.01—27% of the 29.9 GB/s ceiling. Never bandwidth-bound. At q=0.01 the profile is compute-bound (67.7% compute, 2.7% branch flush). As death rate rises the bottleneck shifts to branches: by q=0.5, branch_flush reaches 34.8% while compute falls to 55.1%. The transition occurs around q=0.1–0.25. Bandwidth falls from 8.21 to 4.81 GB/s across the sweep, driven by rising branch cost, not memory.

## Assembly
Zero vector-suffixed instructions—no NEON. Per-particle math uses scalar `fmul s5, s5, s4`, `fadd`, `fsub`, `fcvtzs` on individual `s` registers loaded via `ldp s5, s6`. The scatter does byte-granular read-modify-write: `ldrb w2, [x1]`, `add`, `csel` (clamp to 255), `strb`—three times per pixel for RGB. No gather appears. The `_halide_b5_math` call (`bl`) runs once per step; the per-particle hot loop is entirely scalar. The `ldrb`/`strb`/`csel` scatter with bounds checks (`ccmp`, `tbnz`, `b.lo`) explains both the low bandwidth and the branch-heavy profile.

## Verdict
Refuted — zero vector instructions in step, peaking at 8.21 GB/s = 27% of ceiling at q=0.01. The Halide-expressible loop1 did not yield vectorized per-particle math; scalar `fmul`/`strb` scatter dominates. At q=0.5, branch_flush hits 34.8% and bandwidth drops to 4.81 GB/s, confirming loop2's branchy RNG logic—not memory—is the binding constraint.
